newsitem.title: FRANCE: Maverick Ferrara reworks Jekyll and Hyde in Cannes.
newsitem.headline: Maverick Ferrara reworks Jekyll and Hyde in Cannes.

text.p: The "enfant terrible" of American cinema, Abel Ferrara, sparked a critics' crush at the Cannes festival on Friday with a murky tale of obsession and revenge in which model Claudia Schiffer makes her film debut.

But many film buffs led by publicity photographs for "The Blackout" to expect a lascivious duet of the blonde Schiffer possessively hugging co-star Beatrice Dalle were disappointed. Anyone who blinked missed the scene.

As dark as "Bad Lieutenant" and "The Addiction", Ferrara's latest offering tracks a drug and alcohol-soaked movie star (a nervy Matthew Modine) haunted by his ex-girlfriend (a smouldering Dalle) and unable to reveal his secret to his current partner (a vapid Schiffer).

"Every year Cannes has to have some midnight freak show. This year it is my film...And I will promise you one thing: no one is going to be falling asleep," Ferrara, 46, said of the film shown out of competition.
The crush at an advance press screening was so bad that one woman fainted and the fire brigade had to be called in to assist her. A hundred or so critics failed to find room in the auditorium.

Critics praised Ferrara's technique, untypically bathed in the light of sun-drenched Florida, and packed with flashbacks narrated through super-impressions of images. But the plot itself failed to fuel much interest.

Obsessed by the belief that he may have killed his ex-girlfriend during a drug-induced blackout, the star returns to the scene of the possible crime, which may have been captured by an oddball video-maker (Denis Hopper, the strongest performance in the film).

"It's Jekyll and Hyde: the story of a guy who has the devil in him. He has blackouts and when that happens he loses control. One time, he kills someone. Another time, he pushes a woman into having an abortion," Ferrara said.
"But deep down, the film is a metaphor on the way we systematically waste the best things that happen in our lives," he said.
Germany's Schiffer, 26, failed to impress the Cannes festival in her silver screen debut.

The model -- named one of People magazine's "25 Most Beautiful People" and US magazine's "10 Most Beautiful Women" as the press kit reminded reporters -- plays the model girlfriend in the star's life, making sure he eats healthily and stays off drugs and alcohol.
Ferrara said he chose Schiffer because he thought she could bring out the kindess and purity that he felt was necessary for the part.
"The great thing about Abel is that he creates an atmosphere of total chaos, and out of this chaoes there's room for you to create practically anything you want," noted Hopper.
The work of the eccentric video-maker, a sort of hard-core version of the 19th century novel "Nana" by France's Emile Zola, features prominently in the film.
"You've got to confront the fact that a lot of people are going to see the film on video," said an unpretentious Ferrara.
"Thank God for video cassettes and video stores and, God forgive me for saying it, Blockbusters (retail chain). I know how few people see a movie in a movie theatre now."
